questions.q: Rs. 2500 is invested at 20% per annum compound interest for 2 years. What is the interest?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: 60 litres of a milk-water mixture is in the ratio 2:1. How many litres of milk must be added to make the ratio 3:1?
questions.e: Milk = 40 L, water = 20 L. Need (40 + x)/20 = 3, so x = 20 litres.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: Find the missing letter: A, C, F, J, O, ?
questions.e: The gaps between consecutive letters grow by one each step: 2, 3, 4, 5. The next gap is 6, and O + 6 letters = U.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: What is 0.25 expressed as a fraction in lowest terms?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: What is 7 factorial (7!)?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: How many ways can you choose 2 items from 5 distinct items?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: What is the remainder when 100 is divided by 7?
questions.e: 100 = 14 x 7 + 2, so the remainder is 2.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: A does a job in 10 days, B in 15 days. Working together, in how many days do they finish?
questions.e: Combined rate = 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 per day, so they need 6 days.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: A car covers 480 km in 8 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.e: Speed = 480/8 = 60 km/h.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: An item is sold for Rs. 900 at a 20% profit. What was the cost price?
questions.e: Cost price = 900 / 1.20 = Rs. 750.

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: An item costing Rs. 500 is sold for Rs. 425. What is the loss percentage?

questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.q: What is 2.5 squared?

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: A is B's sister. B is C's son. How is A related to C?
questions.e: B is C's son and A is B's sister, so A is also C's child — C's daughter.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Ravi walks 4 km north, turns right and walks 3 km. How far is he from the starting point?
questions.e: The path forms a right triangle with legs 4 and 3, so the distance is sqrt(16+9) = 5 km.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If the sum of letter positions gives DOG = 26 (4+15+7), what is CAT?

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Book : Pages :: Wall : ?
questions.e: A book is made of pages; a wall is made of bricks.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Find the odd one out: Apple, Mango, Banana, Potato.
questions.e: Apple, Mango and Banana are fruits; Potato is a vegetable.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statements: All pens are books. All books are chairs. Conclusion: All pens are chairs. Does it follow?
questions.e: Pens are inside books, which are inside chairs, so all pens are chairs follows.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statements: Some cats are dogs. No dog is a cow. Conclusion: Some cats are not cows. Does it follow?
o: Only if all cats are dogs
questions.e: The cats that are dogs cannot be cows, so some cats are definitely not cows.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Five people A, B, C, D, E sit in a row facing north. A is at the left end, E at the right end, C exactly in the middle, and B sits between A and C. Who sits immediately right of C?
questions.e: The order is A, B, C, D, E, so D sits immediately right of C.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Find the next letter: A, C, F, J, O, ?
questions.e: Gaps are +2, +3, +4, +5, so the next gap is +6: O + 6 = U.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If MANGO is coded as NBOHP (each letter shifted +1), how is APPLE coded?
questions.e: Shift each letter forward by one: A->B, P->Q, P->Q, L->M, E->F gives BQQMF.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
questions.e: A doctor works in a hospital; a teacher works in a school.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statement: An ad says 'Buy our soap for glowing skin.' Which assumption is implicit?
questions.e: The ad only makes sense if the advertiser assumes people desire glowing skin.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.e: The pattern is a x (a+b): 3x7=21, 4x9=36, 5x11=55, so 6x13=78.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Pointing to a photo, Sita said: 'He is the son of my grandfather's only son.' How is he related to Sita?
questions.e: Grandfather's only son is Sita's father, and his son is Sita's brother.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: You face south, turn left, then left again, then right. Which direction do you face now?
questions.e: South -> left -> East -> left -> North -> right -> East.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Find the odd one out: Circle, Triangle, Square, Cube.
questions.e: Circle, Triangle and Square are 2D shapes; a Cube is 3D.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Bird : Nest :: Bee : ?
questions.e: A bird lives in a nest; a bee lives in a hive.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If BAD is coded as YZW using reverse alphabet (A<->Z), how is GOOD coded?
questions.e: Reverse each letter: G->T, O->L, O->L, D->W gives TLLW.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statements: No cats are dogs. All dogs are animals. Conclusion: No cats are animals. Does it follow?
questions.e: Cats could still be animals without being dogs, so the conclusion does not follow.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If DOG is coded as 26 and CAT is coded as 24, what is FOX coded as?
questions.e: Each word is coded as the sum of its letters' alphabet positions: D+O+G = 4+15+7 = 26, C+A+T = 3+1+20 = 24, so F+O+X = 6+15+24 = 45.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Mohan is 12th from the left and 8th from the right in a row. How many people are in the row?

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: A man walks 3 km north, turns right and walks 4 km. How far is he from the start?
questions.e: Right triangle with legs 3 and 4: sqrt(9+16) = 5 km.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statements: All engineers are graduates. Some graduates are managers. Conclusion: Some engineers are managers. Does it follow?
o: Only if all managers are engineers
questions.e: The managers could come entirely from the non-engineer graduates, so it does not necessarily follow.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: A's age is 3 times B's age and their sum is 32. How old is A?
questions.e: 3x + x = 32 gives x = 8, so A = 3 x 8 = 24.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If 1 January 2024 was a Monday, what day of the week was 1 February 2024?
questions.e: January has 31 days, 31 mod 7 = 3, so Feb 1 is Monday + 3 = Thursday.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Find the next letter: Z, X, V, T, ?
questions.e: Each letter steps back by 2: T - 2 = R.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Find the odd one out: 121, 144, 169, 180.
questions.e: 121, 144 and 169 are perfect squares (11^2, 12^2, 13^2); 180 is not.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: You face north-east and turn 135 degrees clockwise. Which direction do you face now?
questions.e: North-east is at 45 degrees; 45 + 135 = 180 degrees, which is South.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Fish : Gill :: Human : ?
questions.e: A fish breathes through gills; a human breathes through lungs.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If WORK = 67 (23+15+18+11), what is PLAY?

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statements: Some pens are pencils. All pencils are erasers. Conclusions: I. Some pens are erasers. II. Some erasers are pens.
questions.e: Pens that are pencils are erasers (I), and 'some pens are erasers' converts to 'some erasers are pens' (II).

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: A's mother is B's sister. B has a son C. How is A related to C?
questions.e: A's mother and B are siblings, so A and B's son C are cousins.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Find the missing number: 4 : 20 :: 7 : ?
questions.e: Each number is multiplied by one more than itself: 4 x 5 = 20, so 7 x 8 = 56.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: A, B, C, D sit around a circle facing the center. A sits opposite C, and B sits to the immediate right of A. Who sits to the immediate left of C?
questions.e: Place A north, C south, B west (A's right when facing center). C faces north, so C's left is west: B.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: In a row of 30 students, X is 5th from the left. What is X's position from the right?
questions.e: Position from right = 30 - 5 + 1 = 26th.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Find the odd one out: Run, Walk, Jump, Sleep.
questions.e: Run, Walk and Jump are forms of movement; Sleep is not.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Cobbler : Shoes :: Carpenter : ?
questions.e: A cobbler makes shoes; a carpenter makes furniture.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If TRAIN is written as 20-18-1-9-14 (letter positions), how is BUS written?

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: A girl walks 3 m north, turns right and walks 4 m. How far is she from the start?
questions.e: 3-4-5 right triangle: sqrt(9+16) = 5 m.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statements: All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. Conclusion: Some roses are red. Does it follow?
questions.e: The red flowers might all be non-roses, so the conclusion does not necessarily follow.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If today is Monday, what day of the week is it 100 days from now?
questions.e: 100 = 14 x 7 + 2, so 100 days is 14 full weeks plus 2 extra days. Two days after Monday is Wednesday.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: R is Q's brother. Q is P's wife. How is R related to P?
questions.e: R is the brother of P's wife Q, so R is P's brother-in-law.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statement: The company asked staff to work from home during the flood. Which assumption is implicit?
o: Employees can work effectively from home
questions.e: The request assumes remote work is feasible for these employees.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statement: Company X's profits doubled after launching product Y. Conclusion: Product Y caused the profit rise. Does it follow?
questions.e: The profit rise could have other causes; the statement only shows timing, not causation.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If WATER is coded as XZUDS, how is FIRE coded?
questions.e: Letters alternately shift +1 and -1: W->X, A->Z, T->U, E->D, R->S. So F->G, I->H, R->S, E->D gives GHSD.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Which word does not belong: King, Queen, Prince, Throne?
questions.e: King, Queen and Prince are titles held by people; a Throne is a chair, so it does not belong.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Knife : Cut :: Pen : ?
questions.e: A knife is used to cut; a pen is used to write.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If BLUE is written as 5-12-21-5 (letter positions), how is GREEN written?

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: You face north and turn 90 degrees clockwise. Which direction do you face?
questions.e: A 90-degree clockwise turn from north points east.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Find the next letter: A, D, G, J, ?
questions.e: Each letter steps forward by 3: J + 3 = M.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statement: Only graduates can apply for this job. Ravi applied for it. Conclusion: Ravi is a graduate. Does it follow?
questions.e: Applying requires being a graduate, so Ravi must be a graduate.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: A mother's age is 3 times her daughter's age and their ages sum to 48. How old is the daughter?
questions.e: 3x + x = 48 gives x = 12, so the daughter is 12.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If today is Wednesday, what day of the week is it 10 days from now?
questions.e: 10 mod 7 = 3, so Wednesday + 3 days = Saturday.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: What comes next in the pattern: 2, 6, 14, 30, ?
questions.e: Each term is doubled and 2 is added: 6 = 2x2+2, 14 = 6x2+2, 30 = 14x2+2, so the next is 30x2+2 = 62.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Which diagram fits the sets Cats, Mammals, Animals?
o: One circle inside two separate ones
questions.e: All cats are mammals and all mammals are animals, so the circles nest concentrically.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: If P means +, Q means -, R means x and S means /, what is 18 S 3 R 2 P 5?

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: Statements: All mangoes are fruits. No fruit is a vegetable. Conclusions: I. No mango is a vegetable. II. Some fruits are mangoes.
questions.e: Mangoes are fruits and no fruit is a vegetable, so no mango is a vegetable (I); all mangoes are fruits converts to some fruits are mangoes (II).

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: In a certain code, 2 = 5, 3 = 10, 4 = 17. What is 5?
questions.e: Each number is squared and 1 is added: 2^2+1 = 5, 3^2+1 = 10, 4^2+1 = 17, so 5^2+1 = 26.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.q: You face north-west and turn 180 degrees. Which direction do you face now?
questions.e: A 180-degree turn points to the opposite direction: north-west becomes south-east.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
questions.e: Array elements are stored contiguously, so any index is reached with simple address arithmetic in constant time.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which principle does a stack follow?
questions.e: A stack is Last-In-First-Out: the most recently pushed element is popped first.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which principle does a queue follow?
questions.e: A queue is First-In-First-Out: elements leave in the order they arrived.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Converting an infix expression to postfix is most naturally done with which data structure?
questions.e: Operators are pushed and popped by precedence using a stack, which handles the nesting of parentheses and precedence.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Function call recursion is managed at runtime using which structure?
questions.e: Each recursive call pushes a new activation record onto the call stack; returns pop them.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the head of a singly linked list?
questions.e: Only a few pointer updates are needed at the head, independent of list size.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Binary search requires the array to be in what state?
questions.e: Binary search halves the search space by comparing with the middle element, which only works on sorted data.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on n elements?
questions.e: Each step halves the search space, so at most log2(n) comparisons are needed.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the height of a balanced binary search tree with n nodes?
questions.e: Balancing keeps every root-to-leaf path logarithmic in the number of nodes.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h (root at height 1)?
questions.e: A full tree has 1+2+4+...+2^(h-1) = 2^h - 1 nodes.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits keys in sorted order?
questions.e: Inorder visits left subtree, node, right subtree, which yields ascending order in a BST.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: In which traversal order are the nodes of a postorder traversal visited?
questions.e: Postorder processes both subtrees before the node itself.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which traversal visits the root before its children?
questions.e: Preorder visits root, then left, then right subtree.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: In a max-heap, what is the relationship between a parent and its children?
questions.e: The max-heap property requires every parent to be at least as large as its children.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the time complexity of extracting the maximum from a max-heap of n elements?
questions.e: Removing the root requires re-heapifying down the tree, which takes logarithmic time.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the time complexity of building a heap from n unordered elements?
questions.e: Bottom-up heapify works in linear time because most nodes are near the leaves.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the average-case time complexity of a lookup in a well-designed hash table?
questions.e: With a good hash function and low load factor, lookups need only constant expected probes.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which of the following is a collision-resolution technique for hash tables?
questions.e: Chaining stores all keys hashing to the same slot in a linked list at that slot.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A queue implemented with two stacks has what amortized dequeue cost?
questions.e: Elements are moved between stacks at most once each, giving constant amortized cost.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the main advantage of a circular queue over a linear queue using an array?
questions.e: Wrapping the rear pointer around lets the queue reuse slots freed by dequeues.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What operations does a deque support?
o: Insert and delete at both ends
questions.e: A double-ended queue allows insertion and deletion at both the front and the rear.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which representation is most space-efficient for a sparse matrix?
questions.e: Storing only non-zero elements as (row, col, value) triplets avoids wasting space on zeros.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: How much space does an adjacency matrix use for a graph with V vertices?
questions.e: The matrix has V rows and V columns regardless of the number of edges.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: How much space does an adjacency list use for a graph with V vertices and E edges?
questions.e: Each vertex stores a list of its neighbors, totaling V lists and E entries.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Breadth-first search is implemented using which auxiliary structure?
questions.e: BFS explores vertices level by level, and a queue preserves that ordering.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Depth-first search is implemented using which auxiliary structure?
questions.e: DFS goes deep first; a stack (explicit or the call stack via recursion) tracks the path back.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: In a complete binary tree with n nodes, what is the height?
questions.e: A complete tree is as compact as possible, so its height is logarithmic: floor(log2 n) + 1 levels.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A full binary tree has n internal nodes. How many leaf nodes does it have?
questions.e: In a full binary tree (every internal node has 2 children), leaves = internal nodes + 1.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: In an AVL tree, what balance factors are allowed for any node?
questions.e: AVL trees maintain the height difference of subtrees within {-1, 0, 1} via rotations.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which property holds for every red-black tree?
o: Every red node has black children
questions.e: Red-black rules forbid consecutive red nodes, so red nodes must have black children.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: B-trees are most commonly used in which setting?
questions.e: B-trees keep fan-out high and height low, minimizing disk reads for indexed data.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A trie is especially useful for which operation?
questions.e: Tries share common prefixes along root-to-node paths, making prefix queries fast.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Union-Find with path compression and union by rank has what amortized cost per operation?
questions.e: The amortized cost is the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant for all practical inputs.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the time complexity of a range-sum query on a segment tree?
questions.e: The query visits O(log n) segment nodes that partition the range.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) supports prefix sums in what time?
questions.e: Both point updates and prefix-sum queries climb O(log n) tree levels.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the key advantage of a doubly linked list over a singly linked list?
questions.e: Each node stores both next and prev pointers, allowing backward traversal and O(1) deletion given the node.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: How can you delete a node from a singly linked list in O(1) when you only have a pointer to that node (not the head)?
o: Copy the next node's data into it and delete the next node
questions.e: Overwriting the node with its successor's data and unlinking the successor achieves O(1) deletion (except for the tail node).

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which algorithm detects a cycle in a linked list in O(1) space?
questions.e: A slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two steps must meet if a cycle exists.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the time complexity of reversing a singly linked list?
questions.e: Each of the n links is reversed exactly once.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A 'stack overflow' error at runtime most commonly means what?
questions.e: Deep or infinite recursion exhausts the fixed-size call stack.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the value of the postfix expression '2 3 + 5 *'?

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the postfix form of the infix expression a + b * c?
questions.e: Multiplication has higher precedence: b*c is computed first, giving a b c * +.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: In a queue, elements are added at the ____ and removed from the ____.
questions.e: Enqueue happens at the rear and dequeue at the front to preserve FIFO order.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A priority queue is most commonly implemented with which structure?
questions.e: A heap gives O(log n) insert and extract-max/min, ideal for priority queues.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching in a binary search tree?
questions.e: A degenerate (skewed) BST becomes a linked list, so search degrades to O(n).

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Merging two sorted arrays of sizes n and m takes what time?
questions.e: A single linear pass with two pointers merges both arrays.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which of the following sorting algorithms is stable?
questions.e: Merge sort preserves the relative order of equal elements; the others do not guarantee it.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Which sorting algorithm is in-place but NOT stable?
questions.e: Quicksort sorts in place with O(log n) stack space but swaps can reorder equal elements.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: An undirected graph with V vertices has at most how many edges?
questions.e: Each pair of distinct vertices can have at most one edge: C(V,2) = V(V-1)/2.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A directed graph with V vertices has at most how many edges (no self-loops)?
questions.e: Each ordered pair of distinct vertices can have an edge: V choices for source times V-1 for destination.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A tree with n nodes has how many edges?
questions.e: A tree is connected and acyclic, which forces exactly n - 1 edges.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Topological sorting is applicable to which kind of graph?
questions.e: A topological order exists only when the directed graph has no cycles.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: Level-order traversal of a binary tree uses which structure?
questions.e: Nodes are visited level by level, left to right, which a queue enforces.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: What does it mean for a hash function to have a good avalanche effect?
o: Small input changes cause large output changes
questions.e: A good hash spreads similar keys widely, so tiny input changes flip many output bits.

questions.subject: Data Structures
questions.q: A skip list provides what expected time complexity for search, insert and delete?
questions.e: Randomized level promotion gives skip lists logarithmic expected height, like a balanced tree.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the average-case time complexity of quicksort?
questions.e: Good pivots partition the array roughly in half each level, giving n log n average performance.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
questions.e: Badly chosen pivots (e.g., always the smallest) make partitions of size n-1 and 1, degrading to quadratic.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?
questions.e: Merge sort always splits in half and merges in linear time, so it is n log n in all cases.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the auxiliary space complexity of merge sort?
questions.e: Merging requires a temporary array proportional to the input size.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort?
questions.e: Bubble sort makes up to n passes with n comparisons each in the worst case.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the best-case time complexity of insertion sort?
questions.e: On an already-sorted array, each element needs only one comparison, so it is linear.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Selection sort performs how many swaps in the worst case?
questions.e: Selection sort swaps at most once per position, so O(n) swaps despite O(n^2) comparisons.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What are the time and space characteristics of heap sort?
o: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.e: Heap sort builds a heap and repeatedly extracts the max in place, giving n log n time with constant extra space.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Counting sort runs in O(n + k). What is k?
questions.e: Counting sort counts occurrences of each distinct value, so k is the range of possible values.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Which sorting algorithm is NOT comparison-based?
questions.e: Radix sort orders elements by digits/characters without comparing pairs of elements.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search?
questions.e: The target might be last or absent, requiring a scan of all n elements.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Which problem is best solved with the 0/1 knapsack dynamic programming approach?
o: Selecting items with maximum value under a weight limit
questions.e: 0/1 knapsack chooses a subset of indivisible items maximizing value within capacity, solved by DP in O(nW).

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The fractional knapsack problem is optimally solved by which strategy?
questions.e: Taking items in decreasing value-per-weight order is optimal when fractions are allowed.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Dijkstra's algorithm is an example of which algorithmic strategy?
questions.e: Dijkstra repeatedly settles the closest unsettled vertex, a greedy choice that is optimal for non-negative weights.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Dijkstra's algorithm does NOT work correctly when the graph has what?
questions.e: A negative edge can offer a shorter path to an already-settled vertex, breaking Dijkstra's greedy assumption.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm using a binary heap?
questions.e: Each edge relaxation may update the heap, giving (V+E) heap operations at log V each.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Which shortest-path algorithm handles negative edge weights?
questions.e: Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times, correctly handling negative weights and detecting negative cycles.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
questions.e: It performs V-1 passes over all E edges.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The Floyd-Warshall algorithm computes what, and in what time?
questions.e: Its triple nested loop considers every intermediate vertex for every pair, giving cubic time.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Kruskal's algorithm finds a minimum spanning tree using which data structure?
questions.e: Kruskal sorts edges by weight and uses Union-Find to skip edges that would form cycles.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Prim's algorithm is used to find what?
questions.e: Prim grows the MST by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge connecting the tree to a new vertex.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: BFS from a source gives shortest paths in which kind of graph?
questions.e: BFS explores in increasing hop count, which equals shortest distance only when every edge costs the same.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Which traversal is commonly used to detect a cycle in a directed graph?
questions.e: A back edge to a vertex currently on the DFS recursion stack proves a directed cycle.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Which of the following is a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
questions.e: Merge sort divides the array in half, conquers each half recursively, and combines by merging.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: By the Master Theorem, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n solves to what?
questions.e: Here a=2, b=2, and f(n)=n matches n^(log_b a) = n, giving the n log n case.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 solves to what complexity?
questions.e: Each step reduces n by 1 with constant work, so total work is linear.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: A recursive function makes 2 calls on half-size inputs and does O(1) work besides. What is its time complexity?
questions.e: This gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1. The recursion tree has n leaves, each doing constant work, so the total work is O(n).

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Kadane's algorithm solves which problem in O(n)?
questions.e: Kadane tracks the best subarray ending at each position in a single pass.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The two-pointer technique for finding a pair with a given sum requires the array to be what?
questions.e: Pointers move inward from both ends based on comparisons, which only works on sorted data.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The sliding-window technique is most useful for which kind of problem?
o: Subarrays with a constraint (e.g., max sum of size k)
questions.e: Sliding window maintains a window over contiguous elements, updating the answer in O(1) per slide.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The N-Queens problem is classically solved using which technique?
questions.e: Queens are placed row by row, backtracking whenever a placement leads to a conflict.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Activity selection (maximum non-overlapping activities) is optimally solved by which strategy?
questions.e: Always picking the activity that finishes earliest leaves maximum room for the rest.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Huffman coding is a greedy algorithm that produces what?
questions.e: Merging the two least frequent symbols repeatedly yields minimum expected code length.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The Longest Common Subsequence of two strings of lengths m and n is computed in what time by DP?
questions.e: The DP table has m x n cells, each filled in constant time.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The minimum-coin change problem (fewest coins for an amount) is typically solved with which approach?
questions.e: Greedy fails for arbitrary denominations (e.g., coins 1, 3, 4 for amount 6), so DP is needed.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The Longest Increasing Subsequence can be found in what optimized time?
questions.e: Patience sorting with binary search maintains pile tops to achieve n log n.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Matrix chain multiplication is optimized using which technique?
questions.e: Optimal parenthesization has overlapping subproblems, solved bottom-up by DP.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Strassen's matrix multiplication runs in approximately what time?
questions.e: Strassen reduces 8 recursive multiplications to 7, giving n^(log2 7) ~ n^2.81.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Binary exponentiation computes a^n in what time?
questions.e: Squaring halves the exponent each step, so only log n multiplications are needed.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to n in what time?
questions.e: Each composite is crossed out once per prime factor, giving the near-linear n log log n bound.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Euclid's algorithm computes the GCD in what time?
questions.e: The numbers shrink at least as fast as the Fibonacci sequence, giving logarithmic steps.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The KMP string-matching algorithm runs in what time for text length n and pattern length m?
questions.e: The prefix function lets KMP skip ahead without re-scanning text characters.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Rabin-Karp string matching is based on which idea?
questions.e: It compares hash values of the pattern with a sliding window hash of the text, updating in O(1).

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What is the worst-case time of naive string matching (text n, pattern m)?
questions.e: At each of n positions, up to m characters may be compared.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: The comparison-based sorting lower bound is which of the following?
questions.e: A decision tree for sorting n items has n! leaves, requiring at least log(n!) = Omega(n log n) comparisons.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Quickselect finds the k-th smallest element in what average time?
questions.e: Like quicksort it partitions, but only recurses into one side, giving linear average time.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Counting inversions in an array can be done in what time using modified merge sort?
questions.e: The merge step counts cross inversions while sorting, adding no asymptotic overhead.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Memoization is best described as which DP implementation style?
questions.e: Memoization recurses naturally and caches results so each subproblem is solved once.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Tabulation is best described as which DP implementation style?
questions.e: Tabulation fills the DP table iteratively from base cases upward.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: A* search improves on Dijkstra by adding what?
o: A heuristic estimate of remaining cost
questions.e: A* prioritizes nodes by cost-so-far plus a heuristic, guiding search toward the goal.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Which problem is NP-complete?
questions.e: TSP's decision version is NP-complete; no known polynomial algorithm exists, unlike the polynomial options.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: What does it mean for a problem to be in NP?
o: A proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time
It can be solved in polynomial time
questions.e: NP means nondeterministic polynomial: solutions are checkable quickly, even if finding them is hard.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Edit distance (Levenshtein) between two strings is computed using which approach?
questions.e: The DP recurrence considers insert, delete, and substitute operations on prefixes.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: 0/1 knapsack DP with n items and capacity W runs in what time?
questions.e: The table has n x W entries filled in constant time each (pseudopolynomial).

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.q: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting works by repeatedly doing what?
questions.e: Kahn's algorithm uses a queue of zero-indegree vertices, peeling them off layer by layer to produce a topological order.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What does ACID stand for in databases?
questions.e: ACID guarantees reliable transactions: all-or-nothing execution, valid state transitions, concurrent isolation, and persisted commits.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which ACID property ensures a transaction is all-or-nothing?
questions.e: Atomicity means a transaction's changes are either fully applied or fully rolled back.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is the primary goal of normalization?
questions.e: Normalization organizes data to eliminate duplicate storage and update anomalies.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A table is in First Normal Form (1NF) when it has what?
questions.e: 1NF requires each attribute to hold a single atomic value, with no repeating groups.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Second Normal Form (2NF) additionally requires what?
o: Every determinant to be a key
No partial dependency on any part of a composite key
questions.e: 2NF = 1NF plus every non-key attribute fully dependent on the whole primary key.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Third Normal Form (3NF) additionally requires what?
o: No transitive dependency of non-key attributes on the key
Every table to have a foreign key
questions.e: 3NF = 2NF plus non-key attributes depending only on the key, not on other non-key attributes.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: BCNF is stricter than 3NF in requiring what?
o: Every determinant to be a candidate key
questions.e: BCNF demands that every functional dependency's left side be a candidate key.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which two constraints does a primary key enforce?
questions.e: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and can never be null.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is a foreign key?
o: A key shared by all tables
The fastest index in the table
An attribute referencing the primary key of another table
questions.e: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity between related tables.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is a candidate key?
o: A minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row
The first column of a table
questions.e: A candidate key is a minimal superkey; one of them is chosen as the primary key.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: An INNER JOIN returns which rows?
o: All rows from the left table
Only rows with matches in both tables
questions.e: INNER JOIN keeps only the row pairs satisfying the join condition.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A LEFT JOIN returns which rows?
o: Rows with no match on either side
All left-table rows plus matched right-table rows
questions.e: LEFT JOIN preserves every left row, filling NULLs where no right match exists.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What does SELECT DISTINCT do?
o: Removes duplicate rows from the result
questions.e: DISTINCT collapses identical result rows into one.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which of the following is an aggregate function?
questions.e: AVG computes a value over a set of rows; the others are scalar string functions.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: How does COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(column)?
o: COUNT(*) counts rows including NULLs; COUNT(column) skips NULLs
questions.e: COUNT(*) counts every row, while COUNT(column) ignores rows where the column is NULL.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is a correlated subquery?
o: A join written as a subquery
A subquery that runs only once
A subquery that references columns of the outer query
questions.e: A correlated subquery is re-evaluated for each outer row because it depends on it.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is the main trade-off of adding an index to a table?
questions.e: Indexes speed up lookups but must be maintained on every insert, update, and delete.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What does a clustered index determine?
o: The physical order of rows on disk
questions.e: A clustered index sorts the table's data pages themselves; a table has at most one.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which data structure is most commonly used for database indexes?
questions.e: B-trees stay balanced with high fan-out, so range and point lookups need few disk reads.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What does COMMIT do?
questions.e: COMMIT makes all changes in the current transaction durable and visible.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What does ROLLBACK do?
o: Undoes all changes of the current transaction
questions.e: ROLLBACK restores the database to its state before the transaction began.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A dirty read occurs at which isolation level?
questions.e: Read Uncommitted allows reading data written by uncommitted transactions — a dirty read.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Two transactions overwrite each other's updates. What is this anomaly called?
questions.e: A lost update happens when concurrent writes interleave so one transaction's change is silently overwritten.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Two-phase locking has which two phases?
questions.e: A transaction acquires all locks before releasing any, which guarantees serializability.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Deadlock between transactions is best described as what?
questions.e: Each transaction holds a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed — a circular wait.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What does serializability of a concurrent schedule mean?
o: Transactions run one at a time
It is equivalent to some serial execution order
questions.e: A serializable schedule produces the same result as running the transactions in some sequential order.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: In an ER diagram, what does a diamond represent?
questions.e: Rectangles are entities, diamonds are relationships, ovals are attributes.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: In an ER diagram, what does a rectangle represent?
questions.e: Rectangles denote entity sets such as Student or Course.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is a weak entity?
o: An entity that depends on a strong entity and has no full key of its own
questions.e: Weak entities (e.g., a dependent) are identified via a strong owner entity plus a partial key.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is denormalization?
o: Deliberately adding redundancy to speed up reads
questions.e: Denormalization trades storage and update cost for faster read queries by pre-joining data.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is a database view?
o: A virtual table defined by a stored query
A physical copy of a table
questions.e: A view presents query results as a table without storing the data separately.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is a stored procedure?
o: Precompiled SQL logic stored in the database
questions.e: Stored procedures run inside the DBMS, reducing round trips and centralizing logic.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: What is a trigger?
o: SQL code that fires automatically on table events
questions.e: Triggers execute on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE to enforce rules or audit changes.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which of the following are DDL statements?
questions.e: DDL defines schema objects; DML manipulates data, DCL controls access, TCL controls transactions.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which of the following are DML statements?
questions.e: DML operates on the data inside tables.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: GRANT and REVOKE belong to which SQL category?
questions.e: Data Control Language manages permissions on database objects.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT belong to which SQL category?
questions.e: Transaction Control Language manages transaction boundaries.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: How do DROP, DELETE and TRUNCATE differ?
o: DROP removes the table; TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly keeping structure; DELETE removes rows selectively
questions.e: DROP deletes the schema object, TRUNCATE deallocates all rows fast, DELETE removes rows with optional WHERE and logging.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Why does the condition 'column = NULL' never match rows?
o: NULL means unknown, so equality is never true; use IS NULL
questions.e: Comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN, not TRUE; IS NULL is the correct test.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which isolation level prevents phantom reads?
questions.e: Serializable isolation (via predicate locking) prevents new rows appearing in a repeated range query; Repeatable Read alone still allows phantoms in many systems.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: In a 1:N relationship, where is the foreign key placed?
questions.e: Each of the many rows references one parent row, so the foreign key lives on the N side.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which normal form eliminates all non-trivial functional dependencies where the determinant is not a superkey?
questions.e: BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key, removing the anomalies 3NF can leave.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which query finds departments having more than 5 employees?
o: SELECT dept FROM emp WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM emp HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
SELECT dept FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
SELECT dept FROM emp GROUP BY dept WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
questions.e: GROUP BY forms department groups and HAVING filters on the aggregate; WHERE cannot use aggregates.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Fourth Normal Form (4NF) deals with which kind of dependency?
questions.e: 4NF requires BCNF plus no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies, e.g., an employee's independent skills and languages.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is a process?
questions.e: A process is an active program with its own address space, registers, and execution state.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: How does a thread differ from a process?
o: Threads share the process's memory; processes have separate address spaces
questions.e: Threads are lightweight units within a process sharing code, data, and files, while processes are isolated.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What does the Process Control Block (PCB) store?
o: Process state, registers, and scheduling info
questions.e: The PCB holds everything the OS needs to manage and resume a process: state, program counter, registers, and scheduling data.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What happens during a context switch?
o: The OS saves one process's state and restores another's
questions.e: Context switching preserves the outgoing process's registers and state so the incoming process can run.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Which scheduling algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time?
questions.e: SJF (shortest job first) is provably optimal for minimizing average waiting time when burst times are known.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Round robin scheduling is best described as what?
o: Each process gets a fixed time quantum in turn
questions.e: Round robin cycles through the ready queue giving each process one quantum, ensuring fairness.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Starvation is most likely under which scheduling policy, and how is it fixed?
o: Round robin; fixed by longer quanta
questions.e: Low-priority processes can wait forever under priority scheduling; aging gradually raises their priority.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Coffman's four deadlock conditions?
questions.e: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait; allowing preemption breaks it.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: The Banker's algorithm is used for what?
questions.e: It grants resources only when a safe sequence exists, keeping the system out of unsafe states.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is a semaphore?
o: A signaling mechanism for process synchronization
questions.e: Semaphores are counters (wait/signal) that coordinate access to shared resources.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: How does a mutex differ from a general semaphore?
o: A mutex has ownership: only the locker can unlock it
questions.e: A mutex is a binary lock with ownership semantics, preventing accidental unlocks by other threads.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is a race condition?
o: Unsynchronized concurrent access producing wrong results
questions.e: When the outcome depends on the timing of unsynchronized accesses to shared data, results become unpredictable.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is a critical section?
o: Code accessing shared resources that must run atomically
questions.e: Critical sections must be protected by synchronization so only one thread executes them at a time.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: In paging, memory is divided into what fixed-size units?
questions.e: Paging splits physical memory into frames and logical address space into same-sized pages.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is a page fault?
o: Accessing a page not currently in physical memory
questions.e: A page fault triggers the OS to load the required page from disk into a frame.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is thrashing?
questions.e: When processes constantly page-fault, the system spends more time swapping than executing.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Belady's anomaly affects which page-replacement algorithm?
questions.e: With FIFO, giving a process more frames can counterintuitively increase page faults.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Which page-replacement algorithm has the lowest fault rate but is impractical?
o: Optimal (replace the page used farthest in future)
questions.e: Optimal replacement needs perfect future knowledge, so it serves only as a benchmark.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: LRU page replacement evicts which page?
questions.e: LRU approximates the optimal algorithm by assuming past usage predicts future usage.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is virtual memory?
o: Using disk space to extend apparent RAM
questions.e: Virtual memory lets processes use more address space than physical RAM by paging to disk.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: How does segmentation differ from paging?
o: Segments are variable-sized logical units; pages are fixed-size
questions.e: Segmentation divides programs by logical units (code, data, stack) of varying sizes.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Internal fragmentation is associated with which scheme?
questions.e: Fixed-size pages leave unused space inside the last page of a process — internal fragmentation.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: External fragmentation is associated with which scheme?
questions.e: Variable-size segments leave scattered unusable holes between allocations — external fragmentation.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is the kernel?
o: The core of the OS managing hardware and resources
questions.e: The kernel handles process, memory, file, and device management in privileged mode.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is a system call?
o: The interface for user programs to request kernel services
questions.e: System calls (open, read, fork) transition from user mode to kernel mode to perform privileged operations.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What distinguishes a microkernel from a monolithic kernel?
o: Microkernel runs most services in user space
questions.e: Microkernels keep only essentials in kernel mode, improving modularity at some IPC cost.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is spooling?
o: Queuing jobs for a shared device like a printer
questions.e: Spooling buffers output so multiple processes can share a slow device without conflict.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is a zombie process?
o: A terminated process whose entry remains in the process table
questions.e: A zombie has exited but its parent hasn't collected its exit status via wait().

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is an orphan process?
o: A process whose parent terminated; adopted by init
questions.e: Orphans are reparented to the init process, which reaps them on exit.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What does the fork() system call do?
o: Creates a child process as a copy of the caller
questions.e: fork duplicates the calling process; the child gets a new PID and copy-on-write memory.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What does the exec() family of calls do?
o: Replaces the current process image with a new program
questions.e: exec loads a new program into the existing process, keeping the same PID.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Which of the following is an inter-process communication mechanism?
questions.e: Shared memory, pipes, and message queues let processes exchange data; the others are unrelated.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is demand paging?
o: Loading the whole program at start
Loading pages into memory only when accessed
questions.e: Demand paging starts processes with no pages loaded, faulting them in on first access.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Copy-on-write optimization is mainly used by which call?
questions.e: Parent and child share pages read-only until one writes, avoiding a full memory copy at fork.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is swapping?
o: Moving a whole process between memory and disk
questions.e: Swapping frees RAM by writing entire process images to disk temporarily.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is multiprogramming?
o: Keeping multiple programs in memory to utilize the CPU
questions.e: While one program waits for I/O, another uses the CPU, raising utilization.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What characterizes a real-time operating system?
questions.e: RTOSes provide deterministic timing for control systems, unlike general-purpose OSes.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is an interrupt?
o: A hardware signal that pauses current execution
questions.e: Interrupts let devices notify the CPU asynchronously, triggering handler routines.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What does DMA allow?
o: Devices to transfer data to memory bypassing the CPU
questions.e: Direct Memory Access frees the CPU from per-byte I/O transfers.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is the correct speed order of the memory hierarchy (fastest first)?
questions.e: Speed decreases and capacity increases down the hierarchy: registers > cache > RAM > disk.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What does the TLB cache?
questions.e: The Translation Lookaside Buffer speeds up address translation by caching page-table entries.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is a process's working set?
o: The pages it is actively using
questions.e: The working set is the set of pages referenced recently; keeping it resident avoids thrashing.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: The producer-consumer problem is a classic example of what?
questions.e: Producers and consumers coordinate via semaphores so the buffer neither overflows nor underflows.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: What is the dining philosophers problem about?
questions.e: Philosophers sharing forks illustrate how circular waiting causes deadlock without careful protocol.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: In Unix-like systems, a higher 'nice' value for a process means what?
questions.e: Nice values range from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest); being 'nicer' yields the CPU to others.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: How many layers does the OSI model have?
questions.e: OSI has 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: How many layers does the TCP/IP model have?
questions.e: TCP/IP uses 4 layers: Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which is the topmost layer of the OSI model?
questions.e: The Application layer (layer 7) interfaces directly with end-user software.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which is the bottommost layer of the OSI model?
questions.e: The Physical layer (layer 1) deals with bits on the transmission medium.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which transport protocol is reliable and connection-oriented?
questions.e: TCP guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery via acknowledgments and retransmission.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which transport protocol is connectionless and best for live video?
questions.e: UDP skips handshakes and retransmissions, trading reliability for low latency.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: How many messages are exchanged in the TCP three-way handshake?
questions.e: Client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client confirms with ACK to establish the connection.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which port does HTTP use by default?
questions.e: Port 80 is the well-known port for unencrypted HTTP traffic.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.e: Port 443 carries HTTP encrypted with TLS/SSL.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which port does DNS primarily use?
questions.e: DNS queries use UDP (and sometimes TCP) port 53.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
questions.e: IPv4 addresses are 32-bit, written as four 8-bit octets (e.g., 192.168.1.1).

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Why was IPv6 introduced?
questions.e: IPv4's 32-bit address space holds only about 4.3 billion addresses, which were being exhausted, so the 128-bit IPv6 was introduced to provide vastly more addresses.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What is the default subnet mask of a Class C network?
questions.e: Class C uses a /24 mask: the first three octets identify the network.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which of the following is a private IP address?
questions.e: 192.168.0.0/16 is reserved for private networks; the others are public or documentation ranges.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What is the loopback IP address in IPv4?
questions.e: 127.0.0.1 refers to the local machine itself for testing network software.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What does DNS do?
o: Translates domain names to IP addresses
questions.e: DNS resolves human-readable names like example.com into numeric IP addresses.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What does DHCP do?
o: Automatically assigns IP addresses to devices
questions.e: DHCP leases IP addresses and network configuration to devices joining a network.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /24 subnet provide?
questions.e: A /24 has 2^8 = 256 addresses minus the network and broadcast addresses = 254.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What is a default gateway?
o: The router that forwards traffic to other networks
questions.e: Hosts send packets destined outside their subnet to the gateway router.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: HTTP is best described as which kind of protocol?
questions.e: Each HTTP request is independent; state like logins is layered on via cookies/sessions.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What does HTTPS add over HTTP?
questions.e: HTTPS encrypts the HTTP exchange, providing confidentiality and integrity.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What does HTTP status code 404 indicate?
o: The server had an internal error
The requested resource was not found
questions.e: 404 means the server could not find anything at the requested URL.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What is the key difference between HTTP GET and POST?
o: POST sends data in the request body; GET encodes it in the URL
GET is encrypted; POST is not
questions.e: GET retrieves with parameters in the URL; POST submits a body, suitable for forms and uploads.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: A router operates primarily at which OSI layer?
questions.e: Routers forward packets based on IP addresses at the network layer.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: A switch operates primarily at which OSI layer?
questions.e: Switches forward frames using MAC addresses at the data link layer.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: How many bits are in a MAC address?
questions.e: MAC addresses are 48-bit hardware identifiers, usually written as six hex pairs.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: The ping utility uses which protocol?
questions.e: Ping sends ICMP echo requests and measures echo replies for latency checks.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: What does NAT (Network Address Translation) do?
o: Maps private IP addresses to a public IP for internet access
questions.e: NAT lets many devices on a private network share one public IP by rewriting addresses on outgoing packets.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which of the following best describes Python?
questions.e: Python code runs via an interpreter and variable types are determined at runtime.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the key difference between a list and a tuple in Python?
o: Tuples are immutable; lists are mutable
questions.e: You can append or modify list elements, but a tuple's contents cannot change after creation.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does the expression [] is [] evaluate to?
questions.e: is compares identity; the two literals are distinct objects, so the result is False (use == for value comparison).

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the output of: a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a)
questions.e: b references the same list object as a, so appending through b is visible via a.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does [x*2 for x in range(3)] produce?
questions.e: The comprehension doubles each value of range(3) = 0, 1, 2, giving [0, 2, 4].

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the result of 'hello'[1:4]?
questions.e: Slicing takes indices 1, 2, 3 (stop is exclusive): 'e', 'l', 'l'.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What values does range(5) generate?
questions.e: range(5) starts at 0 and stops before 5.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the gotcha with def f(x=[]) as a default argument?
o: The same list object is reused across calls
It creates a new list each call
questions.e: Default arguments are evaluated once at definition time, so mutations persist between calls.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does the yield keyword create?
o: A generator that produces values lazily
questions.e: A function with yield returns a generator whose body executes on demand, one value at a time.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: In def f(*args), what is args?
o: A tuple of extra positional arguments
questions.e: *args collects surplus positional arguments into a tuple.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: In def f(**kwargs), what is kwargs?
o: A dict of extra keyword arguments
questions.e: **kwargs collects surplus keyword arguments into a dictionary.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is a lambda in Python?
questions.e: lambda x: x*2 defines a small unnamed function usable inline.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What do map() and filter() return in Python 3?
questions.e: In Python 3 they return iterators; wrap with list() to materialize results.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the purpose of the with statement when opening files?
questions.e: with uses a context manager guaranteeing cleanup (e.g., file close) even on exceptions.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which method acts as the constructor when a class is instantiated?
questions.e: __init__ initializes the new instance after creation (allocation happens in __new__).

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does self refer to inside a method?
o: The instance the method was called on
questions.e: self is the conventional name for the instance passed implicitly as the first argument.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: How do you make class B inherit from class A?
questions.e: class B(A): declares B as a subclass of A.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the difference between copy.copy() and copy.deepcopy()?
o: copy is faster for nested objects
deepcopy also copies nested objects; copy shares them
questions.e: Shallow copy duplicates the outer container only; deep copy recursively duplicates everything.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is a Python set?
o: An unordered collection of unique elements
questions.e: Sets enforce uniqueness and support membership tests and set operations in average O(1).

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: How do sorted(mylist) and mylist.sort() differ?
o: sorted() returns a new list; sort() sorts in place and returns None
questions.e: sorted() builds a new list leaving the original untouched; list.sort() mutates and returns None.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does 'a,b,c'.split(',') return?
questions.e: split(',') breaks the string at each comma into a list of substrings.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does f'Value: {x}' do?
questions.e: f-strings evaluate expressions inside braces at runtime.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is None in Python?
o: A singleton representing the absence of a value
questions.e: None is a unique singleton; identity checks (x is None) are the idiomatic test.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the result of 7 // 2 in Python?
questions.e: // is floor division: 7/2 = 3.5 floors to 3.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does bool('False') return in Python?
questions.e: bool() returns True for any non-empty string. The string 'False' contains characters, so it is truthy and the result is True.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does enumerate(['a', 'b']) yield?
questions.e: enumerate pairs each element with its index, starting at 0 by default.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which of these is the correct way to handle exceptions?
questions.e: try/except catches and handles runtime errors gracefully.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does the finally block guarantee?
o: It runs whether or not an exception occurred
questions.e: finally is for cleanup that must happen in all cases, e.g., releasing resources.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Machine learning is best defined as what?
o: Algorithms that learn patterns from data
questions.e: ML systems improve their performance on a task by learning from examples rather than hand-coded rules.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Supervised learning uses what kind of data?
questions.e: Supervised algorithms learn a mapping from inputs to known correct outputs (labels).

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What is the difference between classification and regression?
o: Classification predicts categories; regression predicts continuous values
questions.e: E.g., spam/not-spam is classification; house-price prediction is regression.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What is overfitting?
o: The dataset is too small to load
The model memorizes training data and generalizes poorly
questions.e: An overfit model captures noise in the training set, so validation accuracy drops.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What is underfitting?
o: The learning rate is too high
The model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern
questions.e: An underfit model has high bias and performs poorly even on training data.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Why split data into training and test sets?
o: To evaluate generalization on unseen data
questions.e: Test performance estimates how the model will do on genuinely new inputs.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What does k-fold cross-validation do?
o: Trains and validates on k different data splits
questions.e: Averaging scores over k folds gives a more reliable performance estimate than a single split.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What does gradient descent minimize?
questions.e: It iteratively steps parameters opposite the gradient to reduce prediction error.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What happens if the learning rate is set too high?
questions.e: Oversized steps overshoot minima, causing loss to explode or bounce around.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Linear regression is used for which task?
questions.e: It fits a line (or hyperplane) mapping features to a real-valued target.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Despite its name, logistic regression is used for what?
questions.e: It models class probabilities via the sigmoid function, typically for binary classification.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Decision trees choose splits using criteria like what?
questions.e: Splits are chosen to maximize purity of the resulting child nodes.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: A random forest reduces overfitting mainly by doing what?
o: Averaging many diverse trees trained on bootstrapped data
questions.e: Ensembling decorrelated trees averages out individual trees' variance.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What does an SVM (Support Vector Machine) maximize?
questions.e: SVMs find the hyperplane with the largest separation from the nearest points of each class.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: KNN is called a lazy learner because it does what?
o: Stores the training data and defers computation to prediction time
questions.e: KNN does no explicit training; it classifies by voting among the k nearest stored examples.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: K-means is an example of which learning type?
questions.e: K-means groups unlabeled points into k clusters by iterative centroid updates.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Naive Bayes makes which strong assumption?
o: Features are conditionally independent given the class
questions.e: The 'naive' independence assumption simplifies the probability computation, often working well anyway.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What does the ReLU activation function compute?
questions.e: ReLU passes positive values and zeroes negatives, enabling deep networks to train effectively.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Backpropagation computes what, and how?
o: Gradients of the loss via the chain rule
questions.e: It propagates error gradients backward layer by layer to update every weight.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What is an epoch in neural network training?
o: One full pass over the training dataset
questions.e: Training typically runs for multiple epochs, reshuffling data between them.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Precision is defined as which ratio?
questions.e: Precision measures, of all positive predictions, how many were actually positive.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Recall is defined as which ratio?
questions.e: Recall measures, of all actual positives, how many the model found.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: The F1 score is which combination of precision and recall?
questions.e: F1 = 2PR/(P+R) balances both metrics, punishing extreme imbalance between them.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Why is feature scaling important for gradient-based models?
o: It keeps gradients stable and speeds convergence
questions.e: Features on wildly different scales distort gradient steps; scaling (standardization/normalization) fixes this.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: What does a transformer-based LLM fundamentally predict?
o: The next token given prior context
questions.e: LLMs are trained with next-token prediction; coherent text emerges from repeated sampling.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which query finds email values that appear more than once in a users table?
o: SELECT email FROM users WHERE COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT email FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT email FROM users GROUP BY email WHERE COUNT(*) > 1
questions.e: GROUP BY collapses rows per email and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps only the duplicated ones; WHERE cannot filter on aggregates.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which of these tasks is supervised learning?
o: Grouping shoppers into segments with k-Means
Predicting house prices from area, location and age of the property
Finding frequent itemsets in grocery baskets
questions.e: House-price prediction uses labelled examples (features plus the known price) to learn a mapping from inputs to outputs, which is the definition of supervised learning.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: A linear regression model reports R² = 0.94 on the test set. What does this mean?
o: The model explains 94% of the variance in the target variable
94% of the predictions are exactly correct
The correlation between every pair of features is 0.94
questions.e: R² measures the fraction of variance in the target explained by the model: 0.94 means the features explain 94% of the target's variation, not that 94% of predictions are exact.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which activation function is most common in hidden layers of modern deep networks?
questions.e: ReLU (max(0, x)) dominates hidden layers because it avoids saturating gradients for positive inputs, is cheap to compute, and still trains quickly.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: In a neural network, the vanishing gradient problem occurs mainly because
o: the learning rate is too large
the batch size is too small
repeated multiplication by small derivatives of saturating activations shrinks gradients in early layers
questions.e: With activations like sigmoid or tanh, each layer multiplies the gradient by a derivative smaller than 1, so gradients shrink exponentially toward the input layers and they stop learning.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which regularisation technique randomly drops neurons during training?
questions.e: Dropout deactivates a random subset of neurons on each forward pass, forcing the network to learn redundant representations and reducing co-adaptation.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: k-NN with k = 1 on the training set achieves 100% training accuracy but poor test accuracy. This is
questions.e: A 1-nearest-neighbour model memorises every training point, so training error is zero while the model generalises badly — the textbook signature of overfitting.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which algorithm is guaranteed to converge to a global optimum for its training objective?
o: Linear regression solved by the normal equation
A deep neural network trained with SGD
questions.e: Least-squares linear regression has a convex objective; the normal equation (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy gives the unique global minimiser, unlike the non-convex objectives of k-Means or deep nets.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: The bias–variance tradeoff says that as model complexity grows
o: both bias and variance stay constant
questions.e: Simpler models underfit (high bias); as complexity grows the model fits finer structure, so bias falls but sensitivity to the training sample — variance — rises.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which metric is most appropriate for an imbalanced fraud-detection problem with 99% legitimate transactions?
questions.e: Accuracy is misleading at 99% majority class; the F1 score balances precision and recall on the rare fraud class, which is what actually matters.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: A confusion matrix shows 90 true positives, 10 false negatives, 20 false positives and 880 true negatives. What is the recall?

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Cross-validation is primarily used to
o: estimate how well the model generalises to unseen data
increase the size of the training set
questions.e: By training and validating on different folds of the data, cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate of out-of-sample performance than a single split.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Data leakage happens when
o: the training data contains information not available at prediction time
questions.e: Leakage means the model sees during training something it will not legitimately know when predicting — for example, including a post-outcome timestamp — inflating performance estimates.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: In gradient descent, the learning rate is best described as
o: the fraction of neurons dropped out
the step size taken along the negative gradient
the ratio of train to test data
questions.e: The learning rate multiplies the gradient to determine how far the parameters move each update; too large diverges, too small crawls.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Stochastic gradient descent differs from batch gradient descent in that it
o: updates parameters using one sample (or a mini-batch) at a time
uses the full dataset for every update
questions.e: SGD computes the gradient on a single example or small mini-batch, making each update noisy but cheap and frequent, which works well on large datasets.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which loss is standard for binary classification with a sigmoid output?
questions.e: Binary cross-entropy penalises confident wrong predictions logarithmically and pairs naturally with a sigmoid output interpreted as a probability.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: For multi-class classification with softmax outputs, the standard loss is
questions.e: Softmax converts logits into a probability distribution over classes; categorical cross-entropy then measures how far that distribution is from the one-hot true label.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Naive Bayes is called 'naive' because it assumes
o: features are conditionally independent given the class
