questions.e: The model applies Bayes' theorem under the strong (naive) assumption that features are independent given the class label, which simplifies computation enormously.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: The kernel trick in SVMs allows
o: guaranteed linear separability of any dataset
implicitly mapping data into a high-dimensional space without computing the mapping
questions.e: Kernels compute inner products in a higher-dimensional space directly from the original features, letting an SVM learn non-linear boundaries without ever constructing the transformed vectors.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which of these is an unsupervised learning method?
questions.e: k-Means groups data by similarity without using any labels, which is unsupervised; the others all learn from labelled examples.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: PCA is mainly used for
o: dimensionality reduction while preserving maximum variance
questions.e: PCA projects data onto orthogonal directions that capture the most variance, reducing dimensions while retaining as much of the data's spread as possible.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: In a decision tree, the split criterion 'Gini impurity' measures
o: how mixed the classes are within a node
questions.e: Gini impurity is the probability that a randomly chosen sample would be mislabelled under the node's class distribution; splits aim to reduce it.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Random forests reduce overfitting of single decision trees primarily by
o: averaging many trees trained on bootstrap samples and random feature subsets
questions.e: Bagging plus random feature selection decorrelates the trees, so their averaged vote has much lower variance than any single tree.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Gradient boosting builds trees
o: sequentially, each correcting the residual errors of the previous ones
in parallel on random data subsets
by splitting on gradients of the features
only after the data is normalised
questions.e: Boosting fits each new tree to the errors (negative gradients of the loss) of the ensemble so far, progressively reducing bias.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which statement about L1 vs L2 regularisation is true?
o: L1 tends to produce sparse models by driving some weights to exactly zero
L1 shrinks weights but never to exactly zero
L1 cannot be used with linear models
questions.e: The L1 (Lasso) penalty's geometry pushes some coefficients exactly to zero, performing automatic feature selection; L2 (Ridge) only shrinks them.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Early stopping prevents overfitting by
o: freezing the first layers of the network
reducing the batch size over time
halting training when validation performance stops improving
questions.e: Monitoring a held-out validation set and stopping when its error starts rising keeps the model at the point of best generalisation.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: A ROC curve plots
o: true positive rate vs false positive rate across thresholds
questions.e: The ROC curve sweeps the classification threshold and plots TPR against FPR; the area under it (AUC) summarises ranking quality.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: An AUC of 0.5 for a binary classifier means
o: performance no better than random guessing
questions.e: AUC 0.5 is the diagonal of the ROC plot — the classifier ranks positives and negatives no better than a coin flip.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: In the transformer architecture, self-attention lets each token
o: attend only to the previous token
weigh all tokens in the sequence when forming its representation
questions.e: Self-attention computes a weighted combination of every token's representation, so each position can incorporate context from the whole sequence.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: The purpose of positional encoding in transformers is to
o: inject word-order information since attention itself is permutation-invariant
questions.e: Attention has no notion of order, so sinusoidal or learned positional encodings are added to embeddings to tell the model where each token sits in the sequence.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: In a transformer, the 'query', 'key' and 'value' matrices are used to
o: compute attention scores between queries and keys, then weight the values
questions.e: Attention scores come from query–key dot products; after softmax they weight the value vectors to build context-aware representations.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) improves an LLM by
o: retrieving relevant documents at query time and conditioning generation on them
questions.e: RAG fetches pertinent passages into the prompt, grounding answers in retrieved evidence and reducing hallucinations without retraining.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: RLHF is used to
o: pre-train a language model on raw text
fine-tune a language model using human preference feedback
questions.e: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback trains a reward model on human rankings of outputs, then optimises the policy against it to align behaviour with preferences.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: A 'token' in LLM terminology is
o: a chunk of text (word piece) the model processes as one unit
a password used for API access
a single neuron in the network
questions.e: Tokenisers split text into subword pieces; the model reads and generates sequences of these tokens, and context limits are measured in tokens.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Raising the sampling temperature of an LLM generally
o: makes outputs more deterministic and repetitive
makes outputs more random and diverse
questions.e: Temperature scales the logits before softmax: higher values flatten the distribution, so less likely tokens get sampled more often, increasing diversity.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Hallucination in LLMs refers to
o: the model copying its prompt verbatim
the model generating fluent but factually false statements
questions.e: Because LLMs predict plausible text rather than verified facts, they can produce confident-sounding statements that are simply wrong — hallucinations.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Prompt engineering is
o: crafting inputs to elicit better behaviour from a frozen model
questions.e: It is the practice of designing instructions, examples and formatting so that an already-trained model performs the desired task well.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Fine-tuning an LLM means
o: continuing training on a smaller task-specific dataset to adapt its behaviour
questions.e: Fine-tuning updates the model's weights on curated examples so it specialises in a domain or follows a desired format, at far lower cost than pre-training.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which embedding property is most useful for semantic search?
o: Similar meanings map to nearby vectors in the embedding space
questions.e: Embedding models are trained so that semantically similar texts land close together (by cosine similarity), enabling meaning-based retrieval.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: The main advantage of CNNs for images is
o: they work only on grayscale images
shared local filters exploit spatial structure with far fewer parameters
questions.e: Convolutional layers reuse small filters across the image, capturing local patterns like edges with parameter sharing instead of full connectivity.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: LSTMs address the weakness of vanilla RNNs by
o: using gating mechanisms that preserve gradients over long sequences
questions.e: Input, forget and output gates let an LSTM carry information across many time steps, mitigating the vanishing gradients that cripple plain RNNs.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: A support vector machine's decision boundary is determined by
o: only the support vectors closest to the margin
questions.e: The maximum-margin hyperplane depends solely on the training points lying on or inside the margin — the support vectors.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Which distance metric is the default in standard k-Means?
questions.e: Classic k-Means assigns each point to the nearest centroid using Euclidean distance and recomputes centroids as means.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Feature scaling is critical before training
o: k-NN and SVMs with RBF kernels
questions.e: Distance-based methods like k-NN and RBF SVMs are dominated by large-magnitude features unless everything is scaled to comparable ranges; trees are scale-invariant.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: A learning curve where training error is high and validation error is equally high indicates
questions.e: When both errors are high and close together, the model lacks capacity or the features are inadequate — classic underfitting.

questions.subject: AI/ML
questions.q: Batch normalisation helps training by
o: normalising layer inputs to stabilise and accelerate optimisation
removing the need for an optimiser
questions.e: Normalising each mini-batch's activations keeps their distribution stable as weights change, allowing higher learning rates and faster convergence.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which layer of the OSI model handles routing between networks?
questions.e: The Network layer (layer 3) moves packets across networks using logical addresses such as IP addresses; routers operate here.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: TCP is preferred over UDP for file transfer because TCP
questions.e: TCP's sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmissions guarantee every byte arrives intact and in order, which file transfer requires.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: How many usable host addresses does 192.168.1.0/24 provide?
questions.e: A /24 leaves 8 host bits: 2^8 = 256 addresses, minus the network address and the broadcast address, gives 254 usable hosts.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: In CIDR notation, 10.0.0.0/8 means the subnet mask is
questions.e: A /8 prefix fixes the first 8 bits, so the mask is 255.0.0.0, covering all addresses from 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: The default subnet mask of a Class C IPv4 address is
questions.e: Class C addresses (192.0.0.0–223.255.255.255) use a 24-bit network portion by default, i.e. 255.255.255.0.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which protocol resolves a domain name to an IP address?
questions.e: The Domain Name System translates human-readable names like example.com into IP addresses through hierarchical resolvers.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: DHCP is used to
o: automatically assign IP addresses and network configuration to hosts
questions.e: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol leases IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways and DNS servers to devices joining a network.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: ARP resolves
questions.e: The Address Resolution Protocol maps a known IP address on the local network to the hardware (MAC) address needed for Ethernet delivery.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which TCP flag initiates a connection?
questions.e: The three-way handshake starts with a SYN segment; the peer replies SYN-ACK and the initiator completes with ACK.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: The three-way handshake in TCP establishes
o: a reliable connection with synchronised sequence numbers
questions.e: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchanges agree on initial sequence numbers and confirm both directions are reachable before data flows.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Flow control in TCP is implemented with
questions.e: The receiver advertises how much buffer space remains (rwnd), and the sender never exceeds it, preventing the sender from overwhelming the receiver.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Congestion control in TCP uses slow start to
o: probe available bandwidth by exponentially growing the congestion window
questions.e: Slow start begins with a small congestion window and doubles it per RTT until loss is detected, discovering capacity without flooding the network.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: AIMD in TCP congestion control stands for
questions.e: After slow start, TCP grows the window additively (about one segment per RTT) and halves it on loss — the AIMD sawtooth that fairly shares bandwidth.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which of these is a connectionless protocol?
questions.e: UDP sends datagrams with no handshake, no ordering and no retransmission; the application accepts possible loss and reordering.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Port 443 is the well-known port for
questions.e: HTTPS listens on TCP port 443 by convention, while plain HTTP uses port 80.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Port 22, 25 and 53 are associated respectively with
questions.e: SSH uses 22, SMTP mail submission uses 25, and DNS queries use 53 — the standard assignments in /etc/services.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: A MAC address is how many bits long?
questions.e: Ethernet MAC addresses are 48 bits (6 bytes), usually written as six hexadecimal pairs like 02:42:ac:11:00:02.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: IPv6 addresses are how many bits long?
questions.e: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, written as eight groups of four hex digits, giving an effectively inexhaustible space.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: NAT allows
o: multiple private-IP hosts to share one public IP address
questions.e: Network Address Translation rewrites source addresses so many devices on private ranges (e.g. 192.168.x.x) can share a single public IP.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which device forwards packets based on IP addresses?
questions.e: Routers inspect destination IP addresses and forward packets between networks; switches forward frames by MAC within one network.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: A switch differs from a hub because a switch
o: forwards frames only to the port of the destination MAC
questions.e: Switches learn which MAC addresses live on each port and forward unicast frames only there; hubs blindly repeat every frame to all ports.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: CSMA/CD is used in
o: classic shared-medium Ethernet to detect collisions
questions.e: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection let early shared Ethernet stations listen, transmit, and back off when collisions were detected.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Wi-Fi (802.11) uses CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD because
o: wireless stations cannot reliably detect collisions while transmitting
questions.e: A radio cannot listen while sending, so 802.11 avoids collisions proactively with RTS/CTS handshakes and random backoff instead of detecting them.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: OSPF is an example of a
questions.e: OSPF floods link-state advertisements so every router builds the same topology map and runs Dijkstra for shortest paths within an autonomous system.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: BGP is best described as
o: the path-vector protocol that routes between autonomous systems on the Internet
an interior gateway protocol for small LANs
questions.e: The Border Gateway Protocol exchanges reachability between autonomous systems using AS-path attributes; it is the routing protocol of the Internet backbone.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: A subnet mask of 255.255.255.192 (/26) divides a /24 into how many subnets?
questions.e: Borrowing 2 bits from the host portion (24→26) creates 2^2 = 4 subnets, each with 62 usable hosts.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Which HTTP method is idempotent and safe for retrieving data?
questions.e: GET only reads a resource; repeating it has no side effects, so it is both safe and idempotent, unlike POST.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: An HTTP 404 status code means
o: the requested resource was not found
questions.e: 404 Not Found indicates the server could not locate the requested resource at that URL.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: HTTP 301 and 302 status codes indicate
questions.e: The 3xx family redirects the client: 301 is a permanent move, 302 a temporary one, with the new location in the Location header.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: Cookies differ from sessions in that cookies
o: are stored on the client, while session state lives on the server
questions.e: Cookies persist small data in the browser and are sent with each request; sessions keep the actual state server-side, keyed by a session id cookie.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: CORS exists to
o: let servers declare which origins may access their resources from browsers
questions.e: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing uses headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin so browsers can safely permit cross-site fetches the server approves.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: A WebSocket connection, after the initial handshake,
o: falls back to polling every second
provides full-duplex messaging over a single persistent TCP connection
questions.e: After the HTTP upgrade handshake, client and server exchange frames in both directions over one long-lived socket — ideal for chat and live data.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: TLS provides
o: encrypted, authenticated communication over an insecure network
questions.e: Transport Layer Security negotiates cipher suites, authenticates the server via certificates, and encrypts the session against eavesdropping and tampering.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: In the TLS handshake, certificates are used to
o: authenticate the server's identity via a trusted CA chain
questions.e: The server presents an X.509 certificate signed by a certificate authority the client trusts, proving it owns the domain name.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: SMTP is used for
questions.e: The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol transfers outgoing mail from clients to servers and between servers; POP3/IMAP handle retrieval.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: FTP's main security weakness is that it
o: transmits credentials and data in plaintext
questions.e: Classic FTP sends usernames, passwords and file contents unencrypted, so SFTP or FTPS should be used instead.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: A proxy server
o: forwards client requests on their behalf, optionally caching or filtering
questions.e: Proxies sit between clients and servers, relaying requests; forward proxies can cache, filter or anonymise, and reverse proxies front web servers.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: The TTL field in an IP packet
o: limits hops to prevent infinite routing loops
questions.e: Each router decrements Time To Live; at zero the packet is dropped, so misrouted packets cannot circulate forever.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: ICMP is used by tools like ping and traceroute to
o: send error and diagnostic messages at the network layer
questions.e: The Internet Control Message Protocol carries echo requests/replies (ping) and time-exceeded messages (traceroute) for network diagnostics.

questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.q: The main difference between a URI and a URL is that
o: a URL locates a resource while a URI only needs to identify it
questions.e: Every URL is a URI, but a URI may be just an identifier (like a URN) without saying where or how to fetch the resource.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the output of: print([1, 2, 3] + [4])?
questions.e: The + operator on lists concatenates them, producing a new list with all elements in order.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does [x*x for x in range(5)] produce?
questions.e: range(5) yields 0–4, and squaring each gives 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 in a new list.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: In Python, {1, 2, 2, 3} evaluates to
questions.e: Set literals automatically discard duplicates, so the result contains each distinct element once.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the result of {'a': 1, 'b': 2}.get('c', 0)?
questions.e: dict.get returns the default (0 here) instead of raising KeyError when the key is absent.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which statement about Python lists vs tuples is true?
o: Tuples are mutable, lists are not
Lists are mutable and tuples are immutable
questions.e: Lists support item assignment and methods like append; tuples are immutable, though they may hold references to mutable objects.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does the * operator do in f(*args)?
o: Unpacks an iterable into positional arguments
questions.e: Prefixing * unpacks an iterable so each element becomes a separate positional argument to the function.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does **kwargs collect in a function signature?
o: Extra keyword arguments as a dictionary
questions.e: The double-star parameter gathers any surplus keyword arguments into a dict mapping names to values.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: A generator function is distinguished by the presence of
questions.e: Using yield makes the function return a lazy generator that produces values one at a time on iteration.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is printed by: print(list(map(lambda x: x*2, [1, 2, 3])))?
questions.e: map applies the doubling lambda to each element, and list() materialises the result as [2, 4, 6].

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: The classic mutable-default-argument bug occurs because
o: the default object is created once and shared across calls
Python copies defaults on each call
questions.e: Default values are evaluated once at definition time, so a default list accumulates mutations across every call that uses it.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Late binding in closures means that in [lambda: i for i in range(3)], each lambda
o: sees the final value of i when called
captures the value of i at creation time
captures a copy of the loop
questions.e: Closures capture the variable, not its value; by call time the loop has finished, so all three lambdas return 2.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the MRO used for in Python?
o: Determining the order in which base classes are searched for a method
questions.e: The Method Resolution Order, computed by the C3 linearisation algorithm, defines the lookup chain for inherited attributes in multiple inheritance.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which of these creates a deep copy?
questions.e: Assignment and slicing copy only references; copy.deepcopy recursively duplicates nested objects so mutations are fully independent.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does the 'with' statement guarantee for files?
o: The file is closed even if an exception occurs
questions.e: The context manager's __exit__ runs on block exit — including via exceptions — so the file handle is always released.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: In Python, 'is' differs from '==' because 'is' checks
questions.e: 'is' compares identities (id()), while '==' invokes __eq__ for value comparison; small integers and strings are cached, which sometimes confuses the two.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the output of print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)?
questions.e: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, so their sum is 0.30000000000000004, not equal to 0.3.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which exception is raised by int('abc')?
questions.e: The string is the right type but has an inappropriate value for conversion, which is exactly what ValueError signals.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: A decorator in Python is
o: a callable that takes a function and returns a (usually wrapped) function
questions.e: Decorators like @timer receive the decorated function and return a replacement, typically adding behaviour around the original call.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b', 'c']) produce when fully consumed?
questions.e: zip stops at the shortest iterable, pairing 1 with 'a' and 2 with 'b' and ignoring the extra 'c'.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: In a dict comprehension {k: v for k, v in pairs}, duplicate keys result in
questions.e: Later assignments overwrite earlier ones, so the dict keeps the last value seen for each repeated key.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the time complexity of 'x in my_list' for a list of n elements?
questions.e: Membership testing on a list is a linear scan in the worst case; sets and dicts give average O(1) instead.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which method removes and returns the last element of a list?
questions.e: list.pop() with no argument removes and returns the final element in amortised O(1) time.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does 'hello'[1:4] evaluate to?
questions.e: Slicing takes indices 1, 2, 3 (stop is exclusive), giving the substring 'ell'.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: The GIL in CPython means
o: only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time
questions.e: The Global Interpreter Lock serialises bytecode execution across threads, so CPU-bound threads do not speed up; I/O-bound threads still benefit.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which tool creates isolated Python environments?
questions.e: The venv module builds a directory with its own interpreter and site-packages so projects keep independent dependency sets.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does isinstance(True, int) return and why?
o: True, because bool is a subclass of int
questions.e: In Python, bool subclasses int with True == 1 and False == 0, so isinstance(True, int) is True.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: The expression all([]) returns
questions.e: all() is vacuously true for an empty iterable since there is no falsy element; any([]) is False by the same logic.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is printed by print(sorted([(2, 'b'), (1, 'a')], key=lambda t: t[0]))?
questions.e: sorted orders by the key — the first tuple element — producing [(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')].

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which of these is hashable and can be a dict key?
questions.e: Tuples of immutables are hashable; lists, dicts and sets are mutable and unhashable, so they cannot be dict keys.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which list equals list(enumerate(['x', 'y'], start=1))?
questions.e: With start=1, enumerate pairs 'x' with 1 and 'y' with 2, so the list of tuples is [(1, 'x'), (2, 'y')].

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: A classmethod differs from a staticmethod in that it
o: receives the class as its first argument
questions.e: A classmethod gets cls automatically and can touch class state or construct instances; a staticmethod receives neither self nor cls.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What is the purpose of __init__.py in older Python packages?
o: It marks a directory as a package
questions.e: Historically the file's presence told the import system the directory was a package (Python 3.3+ also supports namespace packages without it).

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: Which string method removes leading and trailing whitespace?
questions.e: str.strip() removes whitespace (or given characters) from both ends; lstrip and rstrip handle one side each.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: What does divmod(17, 5) return?
questions.e: divmod returns the (quotient, remainder) pair: 17 // 5 = 3 and 17 % 5 = 2.

questions.subject: Python
questions.q: The else clause attached to a for loop executes
o: only if the loop finished without hitting break
only if the loop body never ran
questions.e: A for-else runs its else block when the loop exhausts the iterable normally; a break skips it — a handy pattern for search loops.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which normal form eliminates transitive dependencies?
questions.e: 3NF requires every non-key attribute to depend directly on the key; transitive dependencies like A→B→C are removed by further decomposition.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A relation is in 2NF if
o: it is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key
every determinant is a candidate key
questions.e: 2NF builds on 1NF by forbidding partial dependencies: non-key attributes must depend on the entire composite key, not just part of it.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: BCNF is stricter than 3NF because it requires
o: every determinant to be a candidate key
all joins to be inner joins
questions.e: BCNF demands that every functional dependency's left side be a superkey, eliminating the residual anomalies 3NF still permits.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: In a database, a foreign key
o: references the primary key of another (or the same) table
questions.e: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity by pointing at primary-key values in the referenced table, linking the tables together.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which SQL clause filters groups created by GROUP BY?
questions.e: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the aggregated groups afterwards, which is why aggregates cannot appear in WHERE.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees; returns
o: the number of rows in employees
questions.e: COUNT(*) counts every row including those with NULLs, unlike COUNT(column) which skips NULL values in that column.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: An INNER JOIN returns
o: all rows from the left table
only rows with matching keys in both tables
questions.e: INNER JOIN keeps the intersection: rows whose join keys match on both sides; non-matching rows from either side are dropped.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A LEFT JOIN keeps
o: all rows from the right table
all rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right has no match
questions.e: LEFT (OUTER) JOIN preserves every left-table row, filling right-side columns with NULL when no partner row exists.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads but still allows non-repeatable reads?
questions.e: READ COMMITTED only reads committed data (no dirty reads), but a row can change between two reads in the same transaction (non-repeatable read).

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: The ACID property 'Durability' means
o: once committed, a transaction's effects survive crashes
questions.e: Durability guarantees committed changes are persisted — typically via write-ahead logging — even if the system crashes immediately after.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Atomicity in ACID guarantees that a transaction
o: is all-or-nothing: it fully commits or fully rolls back
questions.e: Atomicity treats the transaction as one indivisible unit; a failure midway triggers rollback so no partial effects remain.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A deadlock in a DBMS occurs when
o: two transactions each wait for a lock held by the other
questions.e: Circular waiting on locks means neither transaction can proceed; the system detects the cycle and aborts one victim, usually the cheaper to roll back.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Two-phase locking ensures serialisability by
o: splitting lock acquisition (growing) and release (shrinking) into two phases
questions.e: In 2PL a transaction acquires all locks it needs before releasing any; this discipline guarantees the schedule is conflict-serialisable.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A clustered index
o: determines the physical order of table rows
questions.e: The clustered index defines how rows are physically stored and ordered on disk; a table can have only one, since rows have one physical order.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Creating an index on a frequently-filtered column generally
o: slows down reads and writes equally
speeds up reads but slows down writes
questions.e: Indexes accelerate lookups and joins but every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also maintain the index structure, adding write overhead.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which query finds the second-highest salary?
o: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)
questions.e: Excluding the maximum with a subquery and taking the max of the rest yields the second-highest value; the LIMIT variant is dialect-specific.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A correlated subquery
o: is re-evaluated for each row of the outer query
runs once before the outer query
questions.e: Because it references columns from the outer query, a correlated subquery executes once per outer row, which can be expensive on large tables.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Window functions like ROW_NUMBER() differ from GROUP BY because they
o: compute values without collapsing rows into groups
questions.e: Window functions add a computed column to each row (e.g. a rank within a partition) while preserving the original row count, unlike aggregation.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: The RANK() window function, unlike ROW_NUMBER(),
o: assigns the same rank to ties and skips the next numbers
questions.e: RANK gives tied rows equal rank and leaves gaps (1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE_RANK leaves no gaps, and ROW_NUMBER never ties.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A view in SQL is
o: a physical copy of a table
a stored query that behaves like a virtual table
questions.e: Views encapsulate a SELECT as a named virtual table, simplifying access control and reuse without duplicating data.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: The UNION operator
o: combines result sets and removes duplicates
questions.e: UNION stacks compatible result sets and deduplicates; UNION ALL keeps duplicates and is faster when dedup is unnecessary.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which constraint ensures a column has no duplicate values?
questions.e: UNIQUE rejects duplicate entries in the column (NULLs aside, depending on the DBMS); PRIMARY KEY additionally forbids NULLs.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: ON DELETE CASCADE means
o: deleting a parent row automatically deletes dependent child rows
questions.e: The cascade rule propagates a parent deletion to referencing child rows, maintaining referential integrity automatically.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Denormalisation is sometimes used to
o: improve read performance by accepting controlled redundancy
questions.e: Adding back redundant columns or precomputed aggregates avoids expensive joins at read time, trading storage and update complexity for speed.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: A B+ tree is preferred for database indexes because
o: all data pointers live in leaf nodes linked for fast range scans, with high fan-out keeping it shallow
questions.e: High fan-out keeps the tree only a few levels deep, and the linked leaf level makes range queries sequential — ideal for disk-based indexes.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Write-ahead logging (WAL) means
o: logs are written after the commit
changes are recorded in the log before being applied to data pages
questions.e: WAL writes the intention to durable log storage first, so a crash can be recovered by replaying or undoing logged changes.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: The phantom read anomaly is prevented at which isolation level?
questions.e: Phantoms — new rows appearing between two identical range queries — are ruled out only by SERIALIZABLE (predicate locking); REPEATABLE READ still allows them in most engines.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Which of these is a DDL statement?
questions.e: Data Definition Language defines schema objects: CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE; SELECT/INSERT are DML and GRANT is DCL.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Candidate keys are
o: minimal sets of attributes that uniquely identify a row
questions.e: Each candidate key is a minimal unique identifier; one is chosen as the primary key and the rest become alternate keys.

questions.subject: DBMS
questions.q: Lossless decomposition of a relation requires that
o: the natural join of the decomposed relations reproduces the original exactly
questions.e: A decomposition is lossless-join if joining the fragments yields precisely the original rows — no spurious tuples and none lost.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: A process differs from a program in that a process is
o: a program in execution with its own address space and state
questions.e: A program is passive code on disk; a process is its active execution instance, with a PCB, registers, stack and heap.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: The PCB stores
o: process state, program counter, registers, memory limits and scheduling info
questions.e: The Process Control Block is the OS's per-process record: state, PC, CPU registers, memory management and accounting data for context switches.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: A context switch occurs when
o: the CPU saves one process's state and loads another's
questions.e: Switching processes requires saving registers and the program counter into the outgoing PCB and restoring the incoming one's — pure overhead.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Which scheduling algorithm can cause starvation?
questions.e: SJF always prefers short jobs, so a stream of short arrivals can delay a long job indefinitely; aging counters this.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Round Robin scheduling is well suited to
o: time-sharing systems needing fair CPU slices
questions.e: Fixed time quanta rotate the CPU among ready processes, giving responsive, fair sharing at the cost of context-switch overhead.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: A terminated child still shows up in ps output because
o: the parent has not yet collected its exit status with wait()
its code segment was never freed
questions.e: The exited child lingers as a zombie entry holding its exit code until the parent reaps it with wait(); only then is the process-table slot freed.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: The fork() system call
o: creates a child process as a copy of the caller
questions.e: fork duplicates the calling process; both continue after the call, distinguished by the return value (0 in the child, child PID in the parent).

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: exec() differs from fork() in that exec()
o: replaces the current process image with a new program
questions.e: The exec family loads a new executable into the existing process, replacing code and data segments while keeping the same PID.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: A race condition arises when
o: two processes compete for CPU time
the outcome depends on the uncontrolled timing of concurrent accesses to shared data
questions.e: Without synchronisation, interleavings of reads and writes to shared state produce nondeterministic, incorrect results.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: A mutex differs from a binary semaphore in that a mutex
o: can be signalled by any thread
has ownership: only the locking thread may unlock it
questions.e: Mutexes encode ownership for mutual exclusion of critical sections; semaphores are general counters signallable by anyone.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: The necessary conditions for deadlock (Coffman) include
o: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait
questions.e: All four Coffman conditions must hold for deadlock; breaking any one (e.g. allowing preemption or imposing lock ordering) prevents it.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Banker's algorithm is used for
o: deadlock avoidance by checking safe states before granting resources
questions.e: Before allocating, the Banker's algorithm simulates whether a safe sequence still exists; if not, the request waits, avoiding deadlock.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Thrashing occurs when
o: the system spends more time paging than executing due to excessive page faults
questions.e: With too many processes competing for too little RAM, pages are constantly swapped in and out and useful work collapses.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: The optimal page replacement algorithm
o: is used in all modern OSes
replaces the page not used for the longest future time, serving as an unreachable theoretical benchmark
questions.e: Belady's optimal algorithm needs future knowledge, so it cannot be implemented; it benchmarks practical algorithms like LRU.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: LRU page replacement approximates locality by evicting
o: the page unused for the longest time
questions.e: Least Recently Used exploits temporal locality — recently touched pages are likely to be touched again — though exact LRU is costly to track.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: A TLB miss means
o: the page is not in RAM
the translation was not cached, so a slower page-table walk is needed
questions.e: The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent virtual-to-physical mappings; a miss forces walking the page tables in memory.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Demand paging loads pages
o: only when first referenced, on a page fault
questions.e: Lazy loading keeps initial memory small: the first access to a page triggers a fault and the OS fetches it from disk then.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Copy-on-write after fork() means
o: parent and child share pages until one writes, then the page is duplicated
questions.e: Sharing read-only pages after fork avoids copying the whole address space; only a write triggers a private copy, making fork cheap.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: In paging, internal fragmentation is
o: unused space inside the last page frame of a process
questions.e: Because allocation is in fixed-size pages, the final page of a process is usually partly empty — on average half a page is wasted per process.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Segmentation differs from paging in that segmentation
o: divides memory into variable-sized logical units like code, stack and heap
questions.e: Segments match the program's logical structure (code, data, stack) with variable sizes, at the cost of external fragmentation.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: The SSTF disk scheduling algorithm
o: always serves the request nearest the current head position
questions.e: Shortest Seek Time First minimises head movement per request but can starve far-away requests under heavy load near the head.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: SCAN (elevator) disk scheduling
o: sweeps the head in one direction servicing requests, then reverses
questions.e: The elevator algorithm moves steadily across the disk servicing requests in its path, giving bounded wait times unlike SSTF.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: When a user program needs the kernel to open a file or create a process, it invokes
o: a system call, which traps into kernel mode to perform the privileged operation
a plain library function that never enters the kernel
a hardware interrupt raised by the disk
a compiler directive evaluated at build time
questions.e: System calls such as open, read, write and fork are the controlled gateway through which user code requests services only the kernel may perform.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Inode in a Unix file system stores
o: metadata like size, permissions, timestamps and block pointers, but not the name
questions.e: Inodes hold everything about a file except its name; directory entries map names to inode numbers.

questions.subject: Operating Systems
questions.q: Journaling in file systems (e.g. ext4) provides
o: crash consistency by logging intended changes before applying them
questions.e: The journal records metadata (and optionally data) intentions first, so a crash replays or rolls back to a consistent state quickly.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: What does O(n) describe about an algorithm?
o: Its exact running time in seconds
An upper bound on how its cost grows with input size
The average number of bugs it contains
The minimum memory it will ever use
questions.e: Big-O is an asymptotic upper bound on growth rate — it says cost grows at most linearly with n, not how many seconds or bytes a particular run takes.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: A function has two nested loops, each running n times. Its time complexity is:
questions.e: Each of the n outer iterations runs the inner loop n times: n × n = n² operations. Constants are dropped, so O(2n) would simplify to O(n) anyway — but nested loops multiply.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: Binary search on a sorted array of size n runs in:
questions.e: Each comparison halves the search space: n → n/2 → n/4 … reaching 1 in about log₂n steps.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: Which grows fastest as n becomes large?
questions.e: Exponential 2ⁿ eventually outruns any polynomial (n³ included). The ladder order is: log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: The hash-map Two Sum solution uses O(n) extra space because:
o: The map can store up to n entries in the worst case
questions.e: In the worst case every element is inserted into the map before a match is found, so auxiliary space grows linearly with n. There is no recursion or sorting here.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: Two pointers is the natural choice when the input is:
o: A sorted array and you need pairs or ends moving inward
A binary tree needing level order
questions.e: Sorted order lets each pointer step discard one end of the range as impossible, giving a single O(n) pass — e.g. Two Sum II or pair-sum checks.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: A sliding-window solution is O(n) because:
o: Each element enters and leaves the window at most once
questions.e: Both pointers only move forward, so every element is visited a constant number of times — linear total work regardless of window size.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: Why is ''.join(parts) preferred over repeated s += ch in a loop?
o: Strings are immutable, so += rebuilds the string each time: O(n²)
questions.e: Each += allocates a brand-new string and copies everything so far. Appending to a list then joining once copies each character exactly once: O(n).

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: In 'subarray sum equals K', the prefix-sum + hash-map trick works because:
o: sum(i..j) = prefix[j] − prefix[i−1], so a seen prefix of value prefix[j] − K marks a valid subarray
It uses two pointers on the prefix array
questions.e: A subarray sums to K exactly when an earlier prefix sum equals current_prefix − K. One pass with a map of seen prefix sums finds all of them in O(n).

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: Removing duplicates from a sorted array in-place with two pointers gives:
o: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
questions.e: The slow pointer marks the write position and the fast pointer scans once — each element visited once, only a few index variables stored.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: What is the role of the base case in recursion?
o: It speeds up the recursive step
It is the smallest input whose answer is known, stopping infinite recursion
It stores results in a hash map
It converts recursion into a loop
questions.e: Without a base case the function calls itself forever (until stack overflow). It defines the trivial answer — factorial(1) = 1 — that all larger answers build on.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: A recursive function crashes with 'maximum recursion depth exceeded'. The cause is:
o: The call stack ran out of frames — recursion went too deep or never hit the base case
Integer overflow in the return value
questions.e: Every active call holds a stack frame; Python caps the stack at ~1000 frames. Either the base case is missing/wrong or the input legitimately needs deeper recursion (then rewrite iteratively).

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: What distinguishes backtracking from plain recursion?
o: It never uses a base case
It undoes each choice after exploring it, so sibling branches start clean
It always runs in polynomial time
It replaces the call stack with a queue
questions.e: The un-choose (undo) step — path.pop() in the template — restores state before trying the next option. Without it, choices leak across branches and answers corrupt.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: How many subsets does a set of n distinct elements have?
questions.e: Each element is independently in or out: 2 choices × n elements = 2ⁿ subsets. That is also why subset generation is O(2ⁿ).

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: Memoization improves naive recursive Fibonacci from O(2ⁿ) to O(n) because:
o: Each distinct subproblem (fib(k)) is computed once and reused
It uses a smaller stack frame
questions.e: Naive fib recomputes the same subproblems exponentially many times. Caching each fib(k) the first time means n distinct values, each computed once — O(n) time, O(n) space for cache + stack.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: Inorder traversal of a binary search tree always yields:
o: The nodes in reverse insertion order
questions.e: Inorder visits left subtree, node, right subtree. The BST property (left < node < right) makes this exactly ascending sorted order — a favourite interview verification trick.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: BFS uses a queue while DFS typically uses:
questions.e: DFS dives deep: push neighbours and always continue from the most recent — LIFO stack behaviour, which recursion gives you for free. BFS's FIFO queue gives level order.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: For a sparse graph with V vertices and E edges, the adjacency list uses:
questions.e: One entry per vertex plus one entry per edge endpoint: V + E total. A matrix would spend V² cells mostly empty — the standard reason lists win for sparse graphs.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: A BST built by inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order has search complexity:
questions.e: Sorted insertion makes every node the right child of the previous one — a degenerate chain (linked list). Search walks the whole chain: O(n). This is why balanced variants exist.

questions.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
questions.q: Topological sort applies to:
questions.e: A topological ordering (every edge u→v has u before v) exists exactly when there are no directed cycles — i.e. DAGs. It is the classic course-prerequisite / build-order problem.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: Threads of the same process share:
o: The address space: code, data, and heap
questions.e: Threads share the process's memory (code, data, heap) and differ only in their own stack and registers — which is why thread creation is cheap and why shared data needs locks.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: Round Robin scheduling is preferred for interactive systems because:
o: It always picks the shortest job
The time quantum guarantees every ready process gets the CPU regularly
questions.e: Each process runs for one quantum then goes to the back of the queue, bounding every process's wait — responsive, fair, and preemptive by design.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: Which set lists all four deadlock conditions?
o: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
questions.e: Coffman's four conditions must all hold simultaneously for deadlock. Eliminating any single one (e.g. lock ordering kills circular wait) prevents it.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: A context switch is expensive mainly because:
o: Registers, program counter and memory-management state must be saved and restored
questions.e: Switching processes means saving one process's CPU state and loading another's, plus cache/TLB disruption — pure overhead that does no user work, which is why tiny quanta hurt.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: Virtual memory lets a process use more memory than RAM because:
o: RAM is secretly larger than advertised
Pages are swapped between RAM and disk; the process sees a contiguous address space
questions.e: Paging maps a large virtual address space onto smaller physical RAM, with inactive pages kept on disk. The process sees contiguous memory; the OS handles the mapping.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: A LEFT JOIN from users to orders returns:
o: All users, with NULLs where a user has no orders
The Cartesian product of both tables
questions.e: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; unmatched rows get NULLs for right-table columns. That is exactly how you find 'users with zero orders' (add WHERE o.id IS NULL).

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: Adding an index to a table generally:
o: Speeds up both reads and writes
Speeds up reads but slows down writes
Slows down reads but speeds up writes
questions.e: Reads use the B-tree to jump to rows in O(log n); writes must also update the index structure, adding overhead per INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: A table is in 3NF when:
o: Every non-key attribute depends only on the key — no transitive dependencies
questions.e: 3NF forbids transitive chains like student → zip → city. Each non-key column must depend directly on the key, eliminating that redundancy.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: In ACID, Atomicity means:
o: Transactions run on a single CPU core
A transaction's operations all succeed or all fail — no partial commits
Data is stored in atomic data types
Only one user can connect at a time
questions.e: Atomicity is all-or-nothing: if a money transfer debits A but crashes before crediting B, the whole transaction rolls back. The other letters: Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
o: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
WHERE works only on indexed columns
questions.e: WHERE applies before GROUP BY (row-level), HAVING after (group-level, e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5). You cannot use aggregate functions in WHERE.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: TCP is preferred over UDP for file transfer because:
o: It guarantees ordered, complete delivery with retransmission
questions.e: TCP's sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmits guarantee every byte arrives in order — exactly what a file needs. UDP's speed comes from skipping all of that.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: HTTPS traffic by default uses port:
questions.e: 443 is HTTPS (HTTP over TLS); 80 is plain HTTP, 21 is FTP, 25 is SMTP. Ports are the transport layer's way of addressing a service on a host.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: DNS exists to:
o: Translate domain names into IP addresses
questions.e: Humans remember names, routers need numbers — DNS resolves names like example.com to IPs, usually starting from a cached or recursive lookup.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: A 404 status code means:
o: The client requested a resource the server cannot find
questions.e: 4xx = client error; 404 specifically = resource not found on this server. 5xx would blame the server, 3xx would redirect.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: UDP is connectionless, which means:
o: It cannot be used on the internet
It sends datagrams without a handshake or delivery guarantees
It only works on local networks
questions.e: No handshake, no acks, no retransmits — just datagrams. That is why DNS, live video and games accept occasional loss in exchange for low latency.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: Polymorphism lets you:
o: Copy a class's code into another file
Call the same method on different types and get type-specific behaviour
questions.e: One interface (e.g. draw()) with per-class implementations — the caller doesn't care which subclass it holds. That is runtime polymorphism via method overriding.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: 'Prefer composition over inheritance' because:
o: Composition gives flexibility without the fragile-base-class coupling of deep hierarchies
questions.e: Deep IS-A hierarchies break subclasses when parents change. HAS-A lets you swap components (strategies, engines) at runtime with no hierarchy to maintain.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: The Singleton pattern guarantees:
o: A class can never be subclassed
Exactly one instance of a class exists and is globally accessible
questions.e: Singleton controls instantiation so only one object ever exists — the standard fit for shared resources like configuration or connection pools (use sparingly; it hides dependencies).

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: The Observer pattern is the right fit when:
o: Many objects must react automatically when one object's state changes
You need to sort a list
questions.e: Subject → subscribers notification (event buses, model-view updates). Subscribers register interest; the subject pushes updates without knowing who they are — loose coupling.

questions.subject: CS Fundamentals
questions.q: Liskov Substitution Principle requires that:
o: A subclass instance must be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without breaking behaviour
All classes have the same name
questions.e: If code works with Account, it must keep working with SavingsAccount — no strengthened preconditions or weakened postconditions. Violations (e.g. Square vs Rectangle) are classic interview traps.

questions.topic: Machine Learning Basics — Regression to Neural Nets
questions.q: Overfitting is best described as:
o: The model is too simple to learn anything
The model memorized training data and performs poorly on new data
questions.e: High variance: near-zero training error but the learned patterns don't generalize. Diagnosed by the gap between training and validation/test performance.

questions.subject: AI / Machine Learning
questions.topic: Machine Learning Basics — Regression to Neural Nets
questions.q: Logistic regression is used for:
o: Predicting continuous values like house prices
Binary classification — outputting a probability between 0 and 1
questions.e: Despite its name it is a classifier: a linear score passed through the sigmoid squash gives P(class). Continuous prediction is linear regression's job.

questions.q: Why keep a separate test set never used during training or tuning?
o: It gives an unbiased estimate of real-world performance
questions.e: Any data used for decisions (training weights, tuning hyperparameters) is 'seen'. Only a locked-away test set measures how the model does on truly new data.

questions.subject: AI / Machine Learning
questions.topic: Machine Learning Basics — Regression to Neural Nets
questions.q: In gradient descent, the learning rate controls:
o: The size of each weight-update step
questions.e: weight −= learning_rate × gradient. Too large → divergence/overshoot; too small → painfully slow convergence. Schedules that decay it over time are standard.

questions.topic: LLMs & Prompting — How Transformers Are Used in Products
questions.q: The main purpose of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is to:
o: Ground answers in your own documents, reducing hallucinations on private/fresh knowledge
questions.e: RAG retrieves relevant chunks from your corpus and stuffs them into the prompt, so the model answers from provided evidence instead of guessing from training memory — the standard fix for stale or private knowledge.

questions.subject: AI / Machine Learning
questions.topic: LLMs & Prompting — How Transformers Are Used in Products
questions.q: In a transformer, 'attention' lets a token:
o: Weigh which other tokens are most relevant to its meaning
Choose the final output word directly
Compress the model to fewer parameters
questions.e: Attention computes relevance weights between tokens (e.g. linking 'it' to 'animal'), letting each token gather context. Stacked attention layers build the deep representations LLMs reason over.

questions.subject: AI / Machine Learning
questions.topic: LLMs & Prompting — How Transformers Are Used in Products
questions.q: Chain-of-thought prompting ('think step by step') helps most with:
o: Multi-step reasoning tasks like math and logic
questions.e: Forcing intermediate reasoning steps gives the model scratch space to work through problems sequentially — large accuracy gains on arithmetic, logic puzzles, and planning.

questions.subject: AI / Machine Learning
questions.topic: LLMs & Prompting — How Transformers Are Used in Products
questions.q: Setting a low temperature (e.g. 0.2) for factual Q&A is preferred because:
o: It makes output more deterministic and less prone to wild guesses
questions.e: Temperature scales output randomness: low → the model picks the most likely tokens (focused, factual); high → diverse, creative, but hallucination-prone. Factual tasks want low.

questions.subject: AI / Machine Learning
questions.topic: LLMs & Prompting — How Transformers Are Used in Products
questions.q: Embeddings in a RAG system are:
o: Dense vector representations of text, where similar meanings sit close together
questions.e: An embedding model maps text to vectors so semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness — that is what lets the vector DB find 'chunks about refunds' for a query mentioning 'money back'.

oneliners.text: Binary search runs in O(log n) time because each comparison halves the search space.
Merge sort is O(n log n) in all cases but needs O(n) extra space.
Quick sort averages O(n log n); its worst case is O(n²) when pivots are badly chosen.
Heap sort is an in-place O(n log n) sort that is not stable.
Bubble sort's best case is O(n) when it exits early on an already-sorted array.
Insertion sort shines on nearly-sorted data: O(n) best case, O(n²) worst.
Counting sort is O(n + k) for integers in a small range, but costs O(k) extra space.
Radix sort runs in O(d·n) where d is the number of digits — effectively linear.
A hash table gives O(1) average insert and lookup, degrading to O(n) under heavy collisions.
Searching a balanced BST costs O(log n); an unbalanced one degrades to O(n).
Building a heap from an array with heapify costs O(n), not O(n log n).
Breadth-first search is O(V + E) on a graph with V vertices and E edges.
Depth-first search is O(V + E) and can be rewritten with an explicit stack.
Dijkstra's algorithm is O((V + E) log V) with a binary-heap priority queue.
Floyd–Warshall is O(V³) and finds shortest paths between all pairs of vertices.
Kruskal's MST algorithm runs in O(E log E), dominated by sorting the edges.
Prim's algorithm with a binary heap is O((V + E) log V).
Topological sort of a DAG is O(V + E) using Kahn's algorithm or DFS.
Union-Find with path compression and union by rank is amortized α(n) — nearly constant.
Sliding-window solutions to contiguous-subarray problems typically run in O(n).
Two-pointer scans on sorted arrays solve pair-sum problems in O(n) time.
Backtracking explores an exponential O(b^d) search tree in the worst case.
Dynamic programming trades space for time; memoization cuts Fibonacci to O(n).
